Displayed Type Theory and Semi-Simplicial Types
Astra Kolomatskaia, Michael Shulman

Abstract
We introduce Displayed Type Theory (dTT) , a multi-modal homotopy type theory with discrete and simplicial modes. In the intended semantics, the discrete mode is interpreted by a model for an arbitrary ∞ \infty -topos, while the simplicial mode is interpreted by Reedy fibrant augmented semi-simplicial diagrams in that model. This simplicial structure is represented inside the theory by a primitive notion of display or dependency , guarded by modalities, yielding a partially-internal form of unary parametricity. Using the display primitive, we then give a coinductive definition, at the simplicial mode, of a type 𝖲𝖲𝖳 \mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}} of semi-simplicial types. Roughly speaking, a semi-simplicial type X {\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X} consists of a type X 0 {\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0} together with, for each x : X 0 {\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0} , a displayed semi-simplicial type over X {\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X} . This mimics how simplices can be generated geometrically through repeated cones, and is made possible by the display primitive at the simplicial mode. The discrete part of 𝖲𝖲𝖳 \mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}} then yields the usual infinite indexed definition of semi-simplicial types, both semantically and syntactically. Thus, dTT enables working with semi-simplicial types in full semantic generality.



1

Introduction

Semi-simplicial types.

Homotopy Type Theory (HoTT)

[
Uni13
]
is a perspective on intensional dependent type theory that regards types as homotopical spaces or
\infty
-groupoids.
It has proven remarkably successful as a synthetic context in which to do homotopy theory and algebraic topology, and as an internal language for
(\infty,1)
-toposes
[
Shu19
]
.
However, an enduring frustration has been its apparent inability to define general homotopy-coherent structures.
Some infinite structures can be defined in HoTT, such as globular types and spectra; but others, such as
A_{\infty}
-spaces or
(\infty,1)
-categories, have so far resisted all attempts at definition.
We know no convincing explanation for why they should be impossible, but the fact that all attempts appear to fail in a similar way suggests the operation of an as-yet-unarticulated principle.

Specifically, stating an
‘infinite coherence’
property generally seems to require an infinite structure within which to assemble the coherences, while defining such a structure itself seems to require infinite coherence, leading to an infinite regress.
This is in contrast to the situation in classical homotopy theory where the infinite structures to describe coherence, such as operads and simplicial diagrams, can themselves be defined using
strict
point-set-level equalities, which are then automatically fully coherent.
It is tempting to try to mimic this in homotopy type theory using
definitional
equalities in place of point-set ones, but this is difficult because definitional equality is not reified in the theory and we have limited tools for forcing it to hold.

One of the more flexible ways to enforce definitional equalities is to use type dependency, moving from a
fibred
perspective to an
indexed
one.
In the simplest case, this means replacing a function
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}p}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}E}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}
with a type family
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\widetilde{E}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}
.
This has a corresponding projection function
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\pi}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Sigma}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\widetilde{E}}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}
, but we can suppose a point
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\widetilde{e}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Sigma}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\widetilde{E}}
with a definitional equality
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\pi}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\widetilde{e}}\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}b}
by supposing a point
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}e}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\widetilde{E}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}b}
and letting
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\widetilde{e}}=\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}b},~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}e}\right)
.

Thus, it is natural to try to define infinitely coherent structures that can be expressed in a purely indexed way.
The example of this sort which has attracted the most attention is that of
semi-simplicial types
, because they are well-known within homotopy theory and could be used to encode many, if not all, other infinitely coherent structures.
In indexed style, a semi-simplicial type consists of type families
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{0}}
,
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{1}}
,
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{2}}
, and so on, having types that start out as follows:

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{0}}:~

\displaystyle\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{1}}:~

\displaystyle{({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{0}})}~{({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{0}})}\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{2}}:~

\displaystyle{({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 001$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{0}})}~{({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 010$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{0}})}~{({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 011$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{1}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 001$}}~x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 010$}}})}~{({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 100$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{0}})}~{({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 101$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{1}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 001$}}~x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 100$}}})}~{({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 110$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{1}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 010$}}~x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 100$}}})}\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{3}}:~

\displaystyle{({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0001$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{0}})}~{({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0010$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{0}})}~{({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0011$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{1}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0001$}}~x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0010$}}})}~{({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0100$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{0}})}~{({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0101$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{1}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0001$}}~x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0100$}}})}~{({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0110$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{1}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0010$}}~x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0100$}}})}

\displaystyle{({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathfrak{f}_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0111$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{2}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0001$}}~x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0010$}}~\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0011$}}~x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0100$}}~\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0101$}}~\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0110$}}})}~{({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 1000$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{0}})}~{({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 1001$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{1}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0001$}}~x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 1000$}}})}~{({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 1010$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{1}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0010$}}~x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 1000$}}})}

\displaystyle{({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathfrak{f}_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 1011$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{2}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0001$}}~x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0010$}}~\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0011$}}~x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 1000$}}~\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 1001$}}~\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 1010$}}})}~{({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 1100$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{1}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0100$}}~x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 1000$}}})}~{({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathfrak{f}_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 1101$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{2}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0001$}}~x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0100$}}~\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0101$}}~x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 1000$}}~\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 1001$}}~\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 1100$}}})}

\displaystyle{({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathfrak{f}_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 1110$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{2}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0010$}}~x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0100$}}~\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 0110$}}~x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 1000$}}~\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 1010$}}~\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 1100$}}})}\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}

First, we have a type
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{0}}
of
points
. Second, we
have for every two points
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{0}}
, a type

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{1}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}~x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}
of
lines
joining
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}
and
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}
.
Third, for every three points
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 001$}}},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 010$}}},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 100$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{0}}
and
three lines
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 011$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{0}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 001$}}~x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 010$}}}
,
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 101$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{0}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 001$}}~x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 100$}}}
, and
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 110$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{0}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 010$}}~x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 100$}}}
, a type

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{1}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 001$}}~x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 010$}}~\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 011$}}~x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 100$}}~\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 101$}}~\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 110$}}}
of
triangles
with the given
boundary. The pattern continues with
tetrahedra
, which we may also, more
technically, call
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}3}
-simplices. In general,
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}
describes the type of

{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}
-simplices indexed by their boundaries.

Remark 1.1
.

The binary subscripts on variables above follow a scheme that we learned from Tim Campion, although related schemas have been rediscovered many times.
The
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}2}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}}-{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}
simplices constituting an
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}
-simplex and its boundary are labeled by the numbers from
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}
to
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}2}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}}-{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}
written in binary, where the number of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}
s in a binary number corresponds to the dimension of the simplex, and the binary numbers corresponding to the boundary of some simplex are obtained by replacing one or more of the
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}
s in its binary number by
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}
s.
(As we will see later, the binary number
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}
can also be regarded as denoting the unique
({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$-$}1}{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$-$}1}{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$\scriptstyle-$}1}{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}1}}})
-simplex in the boundary of an
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}
-simplex in an
augmented
semi-simplicial set.)

We then list these simplices in the order given by these numbers.
This ordering may seem somewhat curious, compared to the more naïve approach of listing all the
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}
-simplices, then all the
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}
-simplices, and so on; but it does retain the important property that all the simplices in the boundary of some simplex are listed before it (thus, for instance, it makes the semi-simplex category into an
‘ordered direct category’
; see
section

4.5.5
).
We will see later that this ordering is what arises most naturally in (co)inductive constructions of semi-simplicial sets (which was also Campion’s motivation).

In addition to subscripting simplex variables by binary numbers according to this scheme, in this paper we will use different base
letters
to indicate the
dimension
of each variable.
Thus for instance
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 001$}}}
,
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 010$}}}
, and
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 100$}}}
are all
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}
-simplices, while
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 011$}}}
,
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 101$}}}
, and
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 110$}}}
are all
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}
-simplices, and
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathfrak{f}_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 111$}}}
is a
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}2}
-simplex.
We will not have much occasion to denote
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}3}
-simplices; for
({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$-$}1}{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$-$}1}{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$\scriptstyle-$}1}{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}1}}})
-simplices we use the Cyrillic letter

(ze)
.
We may also use different letters from the same alphabets for simplices in different semi-simplicial types, e.g.
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma}_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 11$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}B_{1}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}
and
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\delta}_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 11$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}C_{1}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}z_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}z_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}
.

\triangleleft

One may think of the terms
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{0}}
,
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{1}}
,
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A_{2}}
, and so on as defining the fields of an infinite record type.
Terms of this infinite record type
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}
are known as
semi-simplicial types
.
Thus, the problem is to define a type of semi-simplicial types within homotopy type theory, continuing the above pattern.
As a correctness criterion, one would expect that when interpreted in any
(\infty,1)
-topos the type
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}
becomes a classifier of semi-simplicial objects.
However, even this problem is still unsolved: every attempt to internally encode the combinatorics that generate the type of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}
, as a function of
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}
, seems to lead once again to an infinite regress.

In light of this situation, an alternative approach is to formulate more expressive type theories that can solve the problem of infinitely coherent objects.
One such proposal is
Two-Level Type Theory (2LTT)

[
ACKS23
]
, which introduces an
‘outer level’
of
‘exo-types’
that are not homotopy-invariant.
The exo-types admit a strict exo-equality type, essentially reifying definitional equality, which can then be used analogously to classical point-set equality to define infinitely coherent structures.
And by the results of
[
Usk23
]
, 2LTT can be interpreted in any
(\infty,1)
-topos, so its semantics are not significantly less general than ordinary HoTT, and the type
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}
defined in 2LTT does interpret to the correct classifier.
However, although the exo-equality is assumed to satisfy Uniqueness of Identity Proofs, to keep type-checking decidable it cannot satisfy a reflection rule making exo-equalities into definitional equalities.
Thus, it can be quite cumbersome to work with in practice.

Another proposal is
Simplicial Type Theory (STT)

[
RS17
]
, which changes perspective to view individual types as
simplicial
spaces, with additional primitives for manipulating the simplicial structure.
One can then simply impose conditions on one of these
‘simplicial types’
to make it represent (for instance) an
(\infty,1)
-category.
This suggests a ‘synthetic’ approach to higher category theory analogous to ordinary HoTT’s synthetic approach to homotopy theory, which is potentially quite powerful; and the results of
[
RS17
,
Wei22
]
imply that it can be interpreted in the category of simplicial objects in any
(\infty,1)
-topos.
However, the strength of the synthetic approach is also its weakness: because simplicial types are postulated rather than defined, what we can do with them is limited to what is expressed by the axiomatization.

A coinductive definition of semi-simplicial types.

In this paper we propose a third enhancement of homotopy type theory, called
Displayed Type Theory (dTT)
, in which it is possible to define and work with semi-simplicial types (and many other things).
This type theory is inspired by the following idea for a
coinductive definition
of a type
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}
of semi-simplicial types:

Idea 1.2
.

A semi-simplicial type
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
consists of

•

a type
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{Z}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
, and

•

for each
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{Z}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
, a semi-simplicial type
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}

over
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
.

It may not be at all obvious why this should be a definition of semi-simplicial types, so let us unravel it a few steps:

0.

Every semi-simplicial type
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
has a type
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{Z}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
, whose points we call
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}
-simplices
of
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
.
Thus we may also write
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}={\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{Z}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
.

1.

Every
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}
-simplex
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}
gives rise to a semi-simplicial type
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}
over
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
, called the
slice
of
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
over
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}
.
Of course, if we don’t know what a semi-simplicial type is, we can’t be expected to know what one semi-simplicial type over another one is — at least, not completely.
But we do know that every semi-simplicial type
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
has an underlying type
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{Z}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
, so it stands to reason that a semi-simplicial type
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}

over

{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
should in particular have an underlying type
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{Z}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}

over
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{Z}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
, i.e. a type family
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{Z}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{Z}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}
.
Thus, in particular for every
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}
we have
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{Z}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}):{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}
, hence for every additional
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}
we have a type
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{Z}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x})~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y}
.
We call this the type
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y}
of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}
-simplices
from
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}
to
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y}
.

2.

Now we know that every semi-simplicial type
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
has not only an underlying type of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}
-simplices
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}
, but for every
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}
a type
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}
of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}
-simplices.
Therefore, it stands to reason that any semi-simplicial type
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}

over

{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
should also have, not only a type family
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}
over
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}
, but a type family
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}
over
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}
.
Thinking of
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}
as an indexed representation of a span
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}\leftarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\int}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}
, we deduce that
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}
should be an indexed representation of a span morphism

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\int}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\int}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\int}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\int}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\int}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}}

and therefore we should have

{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}:({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}})~({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}z_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}})~({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}})~({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}z_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}})~({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma}_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 11$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}})\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}.

More precisely, since every
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}
-simplex
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}
of
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
gives rise to a semi-simplicial type
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}
over
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
, any
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}
-simplex
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}z_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}
of
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}
over
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}
should give rise to a semi-simplicial type
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}z_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}
over both
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}
and
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}
.
But the common dependence on
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
should be shared, so
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}z_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}
should live over the cospan
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}\rightarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}\leftarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}
:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}z_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}}

Passing to
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}
-simplices, this means that
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{Z}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}\left({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}z_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}\right)
should be a type dependent on
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}}
,
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}z_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}
, and
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{11}}:({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}})_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}
.
Thus we can define the 1-simplices of
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}
as
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}z_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}z_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma}_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 11$}}}\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{Z}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}\left({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}z_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}\right)~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}z_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma}_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 11$}}}
.

In particular, therefore, since for any
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}
we have a semi-simplicial type
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}
over
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
, we have

\left({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}\right)_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}:({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0})~({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}z_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}:\left({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}\right)_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}})~({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0})~({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}z_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}}:\left({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}\right)_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}})~({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma}_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 11$}}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}})\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}.

Since
\left({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}\right)_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}
by definition, this is equivalently

\left({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}\right)_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}:({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0})~({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}z_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}})~({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0})~({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}z_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}})~({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma}_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 11$}}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}})\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}.

Renaming the variables as
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle ab$}}}\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle ab0$}}}
,
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma}_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle ab$}}}\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle ab0$}}}
, and
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}z_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle ab$}}}\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle ab1$}}}
, and writing
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 001$}}}
, this becomes

\left({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 001$}}}\right)_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}:({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 010$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0})~({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 011$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 001$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 010$}}})~({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 100$}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0})~({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 101$}}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 001$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 100$}}})~({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 110$}}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 010$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 100$}}})\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}.

Thus, this is precisely correct to be a type of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}2}
-simplices:

{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}2}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 001$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 010$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 011$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 100$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 101$}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 110$}}}}\equiv\left({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 001$}}}\right)_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 010$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 011$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 100$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 101$}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 110$}}}}.

This pattern may be visualised as follows:
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{Z}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 1$}}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{Z}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~\left({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}\right)~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 11$}}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{Z}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~\left({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~\left({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 001$}}}\right)~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 010$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 011$}}}\right)~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 100$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 101$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 110$}}}
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 001$}}}
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 010$}}}
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 011$}}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 100$}}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathfrak{f}_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 111$}}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 101$}}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 110$}}}

An alternative, and more geometrical, viewpoint, is that the
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}
-simplex is the
cone
of the
({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}-{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1})
-simplex.
Thus, if we already know that every semi-simplicial type has a suitably indexed type of
({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}-{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1})
-simplices, we can conclude the same about the
n
-simplices as follows.
For every
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}
-simplex
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}
, the dependent semi-simplicial type
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}
has a type of
‘dependent
({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}-{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1})
-simplices’
indexed by the type of
({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}-{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1})
-simplices of
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
.
Thus, an element of this type depends on
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}
(the cone vertex) as well as an
({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}-{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1})
-simplex of
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
(the base face, opposite the cone vertex), and its boundary consisting of dependent
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}k}
-simplices for
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}k}<{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}-{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}
that form cones over all the faces of the base
({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}-{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1})
-simplex sharing the same vertex
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}
.
Together, these form the boundary of an
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}
-simplex.
(In the ordering of variables induced by the above presentation, the simplices in the base face are interspersed with their dependent versions: thus in the case
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}2}
the faces
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 010$}}},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 100$}}},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 110$}}}
form the base
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}
-simplex with
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 011$}}},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\beta_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 101$}}}
the dependent
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}
-simplices (i.e.
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}
-simplices) forming a cone over the boundary
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 010$}}},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 100$}}}
.)
Hopefully this is sufficiently convincing for now; later we will give a precise justification.

As simple and appealing as this
‘definition’
is, it is not meaningful in ordinary dependent type theory.
The intuitive claim is that it defines a type
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}
by coinduction, with
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{Z}}
and
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}
as destructors.
For
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{Z}}
this is unproblematic (it is not even corecursive).
However, the output of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}
is not an element of the type
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}
being defined, as would be usual for a corecursive destructor of a coinductive type, but a
‘dependent element’
, or
‘displayed element’
, of
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}
over the input of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}
.
If we write
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}
for this putative family of
‘displayed elements’
, the types of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{Z}}
and
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}
are

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{Z}}

\displaystyle:\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}

(1.3)

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{S}}

\displaystyle:\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}:\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}\right)\to{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathsf{Z}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}.

We would like to regard this as a sort of
‘higher coinductive type’
.
Just as a higher
inductive
type can have constructors involving not just elements of the type being defined but also
paths
therein, here we have a putative coinductive type whose destructors involve not just elements of the type being defined but also
‘displayed elements’
thereof.
Thus, to make sense of this we need a type theory with a primitive operation
(\mathord{\hskip 1.0pt\text{--}\hskip 1.0pt}){{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}
associating to a type its family of
‘displayed elements’
.
As it turns out, the precise notion of
(\mathord{\hskip 1.0pt\text{--}\hskip 1.0pt}){{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}
that we require is a variant of
unary internal parametricity
.

External and internal parametricity.

In general, by ‘parametricity’ we mean a statement that every type (perhaps subject to contextual restrictions; see below) is equipped with a relation (of some arity), and every function (subject to the same restrictions) preserves those relations.
The original form of parametricity, such as in
[
Wad89
]
, is a meta-theoretic statement
about
type theory, in which the relations are meta-theoretic, and the contextual restriction is that it applies only to
closed
types and terms (those defined in the empty context).
That is, in this
‘external’
parametricity, every closed type is given a relation on its closed terms, which is preserved by every closed function.
For instance, in the unary case, given a closed function
{\left(\right)}\vdash{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}f}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}
, if the
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
-relation holds of a closed term
{\left(\right)}\vdash{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}a}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
, then the
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}
-relation holds of the closed term
{\left(\right)}\vdash{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}f}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}a}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}
.
Indeed, the fact that
f
satisfies this condition is exactly the statement that the
({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B})
-relation holds of it, and is thus a special case of the ‘fundamental theorem of logical relations’ that
every
closed term satisfies the relation on its type.
Semantically, external parametricity is obtained by interpreting type theory in a ‘gluing’ or ‘relational’ model.

By contrast, in type theories with fully
internal
parametricity such as
[
BM12
,
BCM15
,
Mou16
]
, there is no contextual restriction, and the relations are internal (i.e. type families).
In the unary case, this means for any type in any context, say
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\Gamma}\vdash{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}\;\mathsf{type}
, there is a type family that we will denote
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\Gamma},~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}\vdash{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}\;\mathsf{type}
, and every function
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\Gamma}\vdash{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}f}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}
in any context lifts to a function
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\Gamma}\vdash{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}f}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}:({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A})({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}{{}^{\prime}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x})\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}f}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x})
between these type families.
As in the external case, there is a formula for the relation of a function-type:

\left(\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}a}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}\right)\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}~[~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}a}~]\right){{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}f}\equiv\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}a}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}\right)\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}a}{{}^{\prime}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}a}\right)\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~[~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}a}~,{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}a}{{}^{\prime}}~]~\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}f}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}a}\right)

(1.4)

which says that so-called
‘computability witnesses’
for
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}f}
take computability witnesses of
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}a}
to computability witnesses of
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}f}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}a}
.
Thus the statement that
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}f}
preserves computability witnesses is equivalent to saying it lifts to an element
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}f}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}
of this type, and is a special case of a general rule that
every
term
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\Gamma}\vdash{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}a}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
lifts to a computability witness
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\Gamma}\vdash{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}a}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}a}
.
1
1

1

The punning of notation is intentional, and indeed consistent, as we will see: the type
(\mathord{\hskip 1.0pt\text{--}\hskip 1.0pt}){{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}
coincides with the term
(\mathord{\hskip 1.0pt\text{--}\hskip 1.0pt}){{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}
applied to elements of the universe.

Such an internalization of parametricity introduces the new possibility of
iterating
it, leading to
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}
,
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}
, and so on.
Semantically, this means that each type must be interpreted by a
cubical type
(or set), where the arity of the relations determines the number of ‘boundary points’ on each side of the cubes, and the dependencies of each iterated relation on the previous ones supplies the
faces
of a cube.
Our primary interest is in unary parametricity, where
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}
depends only on one copy of
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
; in this case the semantics involves
‘unary cubes’
where each edge has only one vertex.
2
2

2

Geometrically, these can be thought of as powers of a half-open interval
[0,1)^{n}
, or closed octants
[0,\infty)^{n}
in
n
-dimensional Euclidean space.

The rule lifting any
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}a}
to
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}a}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}
then implies that these cubical types must have
degeneracies
, taking any cube to a higher-dimensional one with some boundaries trivial.
More surprisingly, it seems that to have good computational behavior and semantic models, the cubical types must also include
symmetries
(transpositions): from
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}d}\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\lambda}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}.~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}:\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}\right)\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}
, we can either directly obtain the type of
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}d}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}
as
\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}\right)\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}{{}^{\prime}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}\right)\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}{{}^{\prime}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}
or first perform the computation
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}d}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\lambda}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}{{}^{\prime}}.~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}{{}^{\prime}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}
and obtain its type as
\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}\right)\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}{{}^{\prime}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}\right)\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}{{}^{\prime}}
, and it these must be related by a symmetry operation.

The general advantages of internal parametricity over external are clear: we can reason about computability witnesses while staying within a single type theory, using a single proof assistant.
Moreover, internal parametricity allows us to at least try to make sense of a type
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}
with the destructors (
1.3
).
However, fully internal parametricity is not conservative over ordinary type theory: it is highly nonclassical, incompatible with axioms such as the law of excluded middle; and its semantics is not as general as we would like.
We would like our type theory to be interpretable in any
(\infty,1)
-topos (generalizing
[
Shu19
]
), in such a way that our type
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}
is interpreted by a category-theoretic
‘classifier’
of semi-simplicial objects; but as we have just observed, the semantics of internal parametricity seems to live only in a category of cubical objects.
Now the category of cubical objects in an
(\infty,1)
-topos is again an
(\infty,1)
-topos, so (using
[
Shu19
]
) we can expect to interpret an internally parametric type theory in the latter; but the connection of this interpretation to the
original

(\infty,1)
-topos is not clear.

Displayed Type Theory.

Our solution is to use a
less internally
parametric type theory.
We can think of internal parametricity as arising in three stages.
The first stage is an
external
parametricity model, where types are interpreted by pairs
\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A_{0}}:\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}},~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A_{1}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A_{0}}\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}\right)
.
In this case
(\mathord{\hskip 1.0pt\text{--}\hskip 1.0pt}){{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}
maps one model to a
different
model, interpreting an ordinary type by a pair of types; this yields parametricity results as metatheorems.
In the second stage, to make
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}
live in the same model as
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
, we iterate this construction infinitely many times; now types are interpreted by
semi-cubical types
, with faces but not degeneracies.
Finally, in the third stage we add a
‘degeneracy’
operation
\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}\right)\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}
making every
term
parametric.
This allows proving parametricity theorems
inside
the type theory, and semantically moves us from semi-cubical types to cubical ones.

The solution to our problem is to stop after the
second
stage.
This is advantageous semantically because semi-cubical sets are presheaves on a
direct
category (i.e. covariant diagrams on an
inverse
category), and in this case the model construction is much more concrete.
Specifically, in
[
Shu15
]
it was shown that from any model of univalent dependent type theory inside of a type theoretic fibration category, one may form a derived model of Reedy fibrant presheaves on any direct category, with the type formers in the presheaf model constructed inductively in terms of those in the original model.
In particular, in degree
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}
all the type-formers act exactly as they do in the original model.
Thus, semantically we can be sure that all our constructions, including
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}
, specialise to something meaningful in an arbitrary
(\infty,1)
-topos.

dTT is a syntax corresponding to this model, which is likewise intermediate between external parametricity and fully internal parametricity: its parametricity primitive
(\mathord{\hskip 1.0pt\text{--}\hskip 1.0pt}){{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}
has a contextual restriction that is weaker than the
‘only closed terms’
requirement of external parametricity, but stronger than the
‘any context goes’
laxity of internal parametricity.
We start by observing that in either cubical
or
semi-cubical sets, the semantically fundamental parametricity operation actually changes the context: given
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\Gamma}}\vdash{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}t}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
, one has
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\Gamma}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}D}}}}\vdash{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}t}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}t}
, where
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\Gamma}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}D}}}}
augments
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\Gamma}
by computability witnesses of all its variables.
For cubical sets with degeneracies, we can deduce a version of
(\mathord{\hskip 1.0pt\text{--}\hskip 1.0pt}){{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}
that doesn’t change the context by substituting along a degeneracy map
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\Gamma}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\Gamma}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}D}}}}
(e.g. this is the isomorphism between the
‘global’
and
‘local’
models of
[
ACKS24
]
).
But for semi-cubical sets this is impossible, so we have to bite the bullet and deal with context-modifying operations.

The notion of a non-binding operation that changes contexts is familiar from the realm of modal logic, where, to first approximation, a proof of necessity of some proposition, i.e. of
{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\square}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
, may only use necessary assumptions.
Modalities in dependent type theory have previously been used to internalise meta-theoretic operations that don’t make sense in arbitrary contexts, such as the right adjoint to a
\Pi
-type in
[
LOPS18
]
, and we use them similarly here.
Specifically, in dTT we have a modality
{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\triangle\!\square}}
that partially internalises the notion of
‘closed term’
appearing in external parametricity, and which restricts the domain of
(\mathord{\hskip 1.0pt\text{--}\hskip 1.0pt}){{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}
.
Thus the only analogue of the above
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}d}\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\lambda}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}.~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}:\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}\right)\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}
in dTT is
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\widetilde{d}}\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\lambda}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}.~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}:\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}:^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\triangle\!\square}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}\right)\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}
.
In particular, modal variables are protected from alteration
by

(\mathord{\hskip 1.0pt\text{--}\hskip 1.0pt}){{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}
, so that we have
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\widetilde{d}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\lambda}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}.~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}:\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}:^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\triangle\!\square}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}\right)\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}
, thereby avoiding the need for symmetry.

In fact, to emphasise further that dTT retains general semantics over an arbitrary
(\infty,1)
-topos, we will use a multimodal type theory
[
GKNB21
,
GCK+22
]
with two modes, one for the original topos and the other for the topos of semi-cubical sets.
These modes are related by modalities
{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\triangle}}
(the constant semi-cubical type),
{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\lozenge}}
(the
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}
-cubes of a cubical type), and
{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\square}}
(the limit of a cubical type), and
{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\triangle\!\square}}={{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\triangle}}\circ{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\square}}
is a composite endo-modality.
Only
{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\triangle\!\square}}
is necessary to formulate display, but the other modalities are also useful to have around: in particular,
{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\lozenge}}
internalises the process of passing from the model in semi-cubical types to the original model in
\mathcal{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}C}}
.
For instance,
{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\lozenge}}~\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}
is what corresponds semantically to the classifier of semi-simplicial objects in
\mathcal{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}C}}
.

Furthermore, display itself may be thought of as a modality, albeit one that is indexed over the original type.
Display falls into into the new and yet underdeveloped framework of
indexed modalities
, such as the path types of cubical type theory (treated modally in
[
GCK+22
]
) and the identity types of the forthcoming
Higher Observational Type Theory (HOTT)

[
AKS22
,
ACKS24
]
.
Moreover, analogously to those cases, we could formulate display either as an inert type-former defined by abstraction over an
‘interval’
(like path types in cubical type theory), or as an operation that computes on most other canonical type-formers (like identity types in HOTT).
In this paper we make the latter choice, so that rules like
eq.

1.4
are actually definitional equalities.
Formulating such rules computationally is actually easier for dTT than for HOTT, due mainly to the lack of symmetry (although there is a tradeoff, since the presence of modalities is an extra complicating factor).

Until now we have been talking about semi-cubical types to make the connection with parametricity clear, but in the unary case there is an intriging coincidence: the unary semi-cube category is isomorphic to the
augmented
semi-
simplex
category,
3
3

3

To see this geometrically, note that the
({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1})
-dimensional octant
[{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\infty})^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}}
contains a standard face-preserving embedding of the
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}
-simplex,
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Delta}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}=\{({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0},\dots,{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n})\in[{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\infty})^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}}\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}_{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}+\cdots+{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}={\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}\}
, including the augmentation case
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Delta}^{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$-$}1}{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$-$}1}{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$\scriptstyle-$}1}{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}1}}}={\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\emptyset}
.
with a dimension shift: the
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}
-cube corresponds to the
({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}-{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1})
-simplex.
For this reason we refer to the two modes in our theory as the
discrete mode

\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}dm}}
and the
simplicial mode

\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}sm}}
.
Thus, dTT can actually internalise semi-simplicial types in
two
ways: as the coinductive type
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}
mentioned above, and as the
universe
of types at the simplicial mode.
The latter suggests that dTT could also be used similarly to simplicial type theory, with types at the simplicial mode treated as synthetic (augmented semi-) simplicial types.

(Note that an augmented semi-simplicial type can be viewed as a family of ordinary semi-simplicial sets indexed by the type of
({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$-$}1}{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$-$}1}{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$\scriptstyle-$}1}{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}1}}})
-simplices.
Thus, our observation that augmented semi-simplicial types support a better internal language than ordinary ones is analogous to the observation of
[
RFL21
]
that
parametrised
spectra are likewise preferable to unparametrised ones.)

Displayed structures.

Our terminology
display
for the operation
d
is inspired by the fact that when applied to record types whose elements are algebraic structures, it produces
displayed structures
of the corresponding sort.
Here a
‘displayed structure’
over a structure
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}
is a structure
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
of the same kind with a structure map
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}
, but reformulated in terms of the corresponding family of fibres
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}
.
Working with displayed structures rather than morphisms is a technique for enforcing definitional equalities on images in
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}
.

The most common displayed structure is a
displayed category
; here the terminology was introduced by
[
AL19
]
.
This arises from the record type of categories, defined in the usual dependently typed way (where we omit the axioms for concision):

Thus a displayed category over
\mathcal{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}C}}
has a type of objects indexed by those of
\mathcal{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}C}}
, types of morphisms indexed by pairs of objects-over-objects and by a morphism of
\mathcal{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}C}}
, identity and composition operations on displayed objects and morphisms that lie strictly over those in
\mathcal{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}C}}
, and similarly for the axioms.

As observed in
[
AL19
]
, one use of displayed categories is to state definitions such as Grothendieck fibrations in terms of the existence of cartesian liftings strictly over any morphism in
\mathcal{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}C}}
, without internalizing definitional equality.
Another is to construct categories and prove their properties in a modular way out of dependent pieces, just as we do for types using
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Sigma}
-types and more general records.
It is
‘well-known’
by now that any sort of algebro-categorical structure has a
‘displayed version’
— for instance, displayed bicategories were used in
[
AFM+21
]
to prove univalence modularly — but to our knowledge this has not previously been formalised.
Our
Displayed Type Theory (dTT)
automatically generates the displayed version of any notion definable in type theory; hence the name.

Outline of the paper.

The rest of this paper has three parts.
In
section

2
we describe the general syntax of dTT, including the modalities, the operation of display (in various different forms), and how they compute.
We do not prove any canonicity or normalization results, but we conjecture that they hold.

In
section

3
we extend the syntax of dTT to define a type
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}
of semi-simplicial types.
In fact, we obtain this as a special case of a general notion of
‘displayed coinductive type’
, which is easier to work with abstractly, and also includes other important examples such as the type of semi-simplicial morphisms between two semi-simplicial types.
4
4

4

One might hope that it would also include the displayed versions
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}
,
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}
, etc., but this does not seem to be the case unless we add symmetry to our theory.

Then we explore a few applications, to make the point that this coinductive notion of semi-simplicial type is useful and practical.

Finally, in
section

4
we consider the semantics of dTT.
In particular, we will show that from any model
\mathcal{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}C}}
of ordinary dependent type theory with countable inverse limits (roughly as considered in
[
Kra15
]
), we can construct a model of dTT whose discrete mode is
\mathcal{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}C}}
and whose simplicial mode is the category of Reedy fibrant augmented semi-simplicial diagrams in
\mathcal{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}C}}
, and that this model supports displayed coinductive types including a type
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}
of semi-simplicial types.
The underlying ordinary type theory of this model at the simplicial mode is an instance of the inverse diagram models of
[
Shu15
,
KL21
]
, but we construct it more explicitly by hand so as to be able to verify the needed formulas for the additional operations of dTT.

Thus, although dTT is (apparently) not conservative over ordinary dependent type theory, we can isolate exactly a kind of extra infinitary structure that yields a well-behaved theory for working with semi-simplicial types, which precisely includes the original model at one mode.
In particular, by
[
Shu19
]
any
(\infty,1)
-topos can be presented by a type-theoretic model topos, which is a model of type theory with countable inverse limits, and thus also yields a model of dTT.
However, an object with the
internal
universal property of
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}
expressable in dTT has the potential to exist even in models that lack such infinitary limits, which may have implications for a notion of elementary
(\infty,1)
-topos.
