\displaystyle\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}b}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}h}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma}{{}^{\prime}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}ev}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y}{{}^{\prime}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}ev}}}}

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma}{{}^{\prime}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathbb{2}}\times{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}},~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y}{{}^{\prime}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Theta}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}p}^{*}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}}

\displaystyle\vdash_{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}sm}}}

\displaystyle\;{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}b}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}h})}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma}{{}^{\prime}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y}{{}^{\prime}}

\displaystyle\equiv({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}b}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}h}){{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma}{{}^{\prime}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y}{{}^{\prime}}

For the inductive step of
1
, we have

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathbb{2}}\times({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}\oplus{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H})=({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathbb{2}}\times{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I})\oplus({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}i_{0}})_{!}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}\oplus({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}p}^{*}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}\cup\{({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\xi},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}_{\star})\}).

Thus, using
2
, we have

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathbb{2}}\times({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}\oplus{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H})}

\displaystyle\equiv\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma}{{}^{\prime}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathbb{2}}\times{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I})},~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0},\star)}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Theta}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}i_{0}})_{!}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}}\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\ell},~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1},\star)}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Theta}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}p}^{*}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}\cup\{({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\xi},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}_{\star})\})}\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\ell}\right)

\displaystyle\equiv\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma}{{}^{\prime}}:({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}}){{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}D}}}},~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0},\star)}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Theta}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma}{{}^{\prime}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}ev}}}}\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\ell},~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1},\star)}:({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y}{{}^{\prime}}:({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Theta}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}}){{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}D}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma}{{}^{\prime}})\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0},\star)}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y}{{}^{\prime}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}ev}}}}\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\ell}\right)

\displaystyle\equiv\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I},~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\star}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Theta}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma}\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\ell}\right){{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}D}}}}.

The other cases are similar.
We can likewise show that

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathbb{2}}\times{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}}\equiv({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}){{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}},

with the isomorphism
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathbb{2}}\times{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}}\cong\left({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathbb{2}}\times{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}}\right)
coinciding with the evens/odds pairing isomorphism
({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}}){{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}D}}}}\cong\left({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}\mid({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}){{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}\right)
.

4.5.5.5
Discrete fibrations.

The isomorphism
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}\cong\left({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}}\right)
ensures that if
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}
is a sieve, we have a weakening substitution
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}
.
But more generally, we can expect to induce a context substitution from any discrete fibration.
Even more generally, we can get a
partial
substitution from a ‘dependent’ discrete fibration, in the following sense.

Definition 4.57
.

If
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}i}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}\hookrightarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}
is the inclusion of a sieve in a direct category, a
co-section
of it is a discrete fibration
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}p}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}
such that
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}p}\circ{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}i}={\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}
.
In this case, if
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}
is a presheaf on
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}
and
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}K}
a presheaf on
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}
, a morphism
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}K}
over
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}p}
is a
relative isomorphism
if it induces a bijection
\sum_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y}\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y})\to\sum_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y}\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}K}({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y})
.

Note that the projection
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}p}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathbb{2}}\times{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}
above is
not
a co-section of the sieve
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}i_{0}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}\hookrightarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathbb{2}}\times{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}
, since it is not a discrete fibration.
The prototypical example of a relative isomorphism is
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\partial\!{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\text{\char 136\relax}}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\partial\!{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\text{\char 136\relax}}}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}p}({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x})}
for any
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}
(this is essentially the definition of a discrete fibration).

Now we define and prove inductively:

1.

For any co-section
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}p}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}
of a sieve
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}i}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}\hookrightarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}
in an ordered direct category, a partial substitution
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}\vdash_{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}sm}}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}p}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}}
.

2.

In addition, for any order-preserving relative isomorphism
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}K}
between ordered presheaves, we have
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Theta}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}[~{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}p}}~]\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Theta}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}K}
.

3.

For
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}
, we have
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}B}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}[~{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}p}}~]\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}B}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}p}({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x})}
.

4.

For
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\alpha}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}K}
an order-preserving relative isomorphism and
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}h}\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}(x)
, we have
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}b}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}}[~{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}p}}~]\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}b}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\alpha}({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x})}
.

To construct
1
, note that as before there are two possibilities for a sieve in
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}\oplus{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}
: it can be
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}
or
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}\oplus{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}
for a sieve
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}
in
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}
.
In the latter case, we have
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}\oplus{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H},~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}\oplus{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}}={\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}}
weakened to
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}\oplus{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}}
, and a co-section of
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}\oplus{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}\hookrightarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}\oplus{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}
is determined by a co-section
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}p}
of
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}
; thus we can similarly weaken
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}p}}
.

In the former case, a co-section
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}\oplus{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}
is determined by a co-section
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}p}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}
together with an object
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}
and a relative isomorphism
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\partial\!{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\text{\char 136\relax}}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}
.
Since
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J},~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}\oplus{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}}=\left({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}},~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\star}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Theta}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\ell}\right)
in this case, to extend
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}p}}
as desired it suffices to give a term of type
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}\vdash_{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}sm}}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Theta}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}[~{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}p}}~]\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\ell}
.
But using
2
inductively, this is equal to
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}\vdash_{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}sm}}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Theta}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\partial\!{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\text{\char 136\relax}}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}}\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\ell}
, so we can use the variable
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}
in
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}
.

Now to prove
2
, we induct on the ordering of
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}
and
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}K}
, inductively using
3
.
The inductive arguments for
3
–
4
are similar.

4.5.5.6
Categorical coning.

Our last generic construction is a category-theoretic notion of ‘coning’ a direct category.
Let
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}
be a sieve in a direct category that contains the bottom object, which we presciently denote
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}}
.
Let
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}+}}
denote the direct category
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}
augmented by an additional morphism
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\zeta}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}
for all objects
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}\setminus{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}
.
9
9

9

The notation is somewhat abusive, since the construction depends on
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}
as well as
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}
.

We define
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}f}\circ{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\zeta}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}={\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\zeta}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y}
for all
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}f}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y}
; note that
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}\setminus{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}
implies
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}y}\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}\setminus{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}
since
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}
is a sieve.
If
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}
is ordered, we order
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}+}}
by placing
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\zeta}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}

before
all other morphisms with codomain
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}
; this is actually the only possibility given our definition of composition.
Note that
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}
is still a sieve in
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}+}}
.

Similarly, for a presheaf
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}
on
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}
, let
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}+}}
denote the presheaf on
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}+}}
consisting of
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}
augmented by a new element
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\zeta}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}})
, such that
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}+}}({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\zeta}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x})({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}h})={\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\zeta}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}
for all
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}h}\in{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x})
.
If
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}
is ordered, we order
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}+}}
by putting
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\zeta}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}
first.

We now inductively prove:

1.

For any sieve
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}
in an ordered direct category, we have
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}+}}}\equiv({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}z}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}B}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}}})\to{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}}
(meaning a
\Pi
-telescope).

2.

In addition, for any
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}
on
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}
, if we transfer
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Theta}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}
and
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Theta}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}+}}}
across the isomorphisms

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}}

\displaystyle\cong\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\delta}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma}\right)

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}+}}}

\displaystyle\cong\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\delta}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}+}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma}\right)\equiv\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J}\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\delta}:({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}z}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}B}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma})\to{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}J},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma}\right)

to get
\smash{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\tilde{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Theta}}}}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}
and
\smash{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\tilde{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Theta}}}}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}+}}}
, then we have

\smash{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\tilde{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Theta}}}}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}+}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\delta}\equiv\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}z}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}B}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma},~\smash{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\tilde{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Theta}}}}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\gamma}~\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\delta}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}z}\right)\right)

Both proofs are entirely straightforward, using the inductive definition of
\Pi
-telescopes as well as
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}I}
and
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Theta}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}
.

4.5.5.7
Correctness of semi-simplicial types.

Recall that our definition of semi-simplicial types
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\ell}}
is as a displayed coinductive type with
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\Phi}\equiv{\left(\right)}
,
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}\equiv\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\ell}
, and
\mathcal{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}a}\equiv\left(x:\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}El}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}a}\right)
.
Therefore, the construction in
section

4.5.2
simplifies as follows:

\vdash_{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}sm}}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}}\;\mathsf{tel}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}}\vdash_{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}sm}}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}\;\mathsf{tel}\vdash_{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}sm}}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\partial ,1}x}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}},~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x},~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}b}:\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}El}}~({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}h}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x})\vdash_{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}sm}}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}t}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}b}:({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}}){{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}},~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}b}:\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}El}}~({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}h}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x})\vdash_{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}sm}}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}t}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}b}\equiv[~~]

{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}},~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x},~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}{{}^{\prime}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}}~[~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}~],~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}b}:\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}El}}~({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}h}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x})\vdash_{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}sm}}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}t}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}}~[~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}~]~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}{{}^{\prime}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}b}\equiv[~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}t}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}b},~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}{{}^{\prime}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}b}~]

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}},~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}

\displaystyle\vdash_{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}sm}}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}}~[~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x},~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}~]\equiv({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}b}:\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}El}}~({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}h}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}-{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}))\to({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}){{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}\;{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}\;{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{,}}\;{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}t}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}b}\;{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}

We will prove inductively that

{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}}\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Delta_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$-$}1}{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$-$}1}{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$\scriptstyle-$}1}{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}1}}}}}}\quad\text{and}\quad{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Theta}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\partial\!{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\text{\char 136\relax}}}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}}}}\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\ell}.

This will imply that
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}=\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}lim}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}}
is a classifying context for all of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Delta}
.
The claim about
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}
clearly inductively implies the claim about
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}}
.
Also it is easy to show inductively that
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}h}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}B}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}}}
.
So it remains to say something useful about
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}t}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}
.

Let
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}I}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}
be the subcategory of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathbb{2}}\times{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Delta_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}}}
containing all the objects except
({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}})
, and let
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}J}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}=\{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}\}\times{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Delta_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}}}
regarded as a sieve in
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}I}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}
.
The central fact is the following.

Lemma 4.58
.

For any
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}
, there is a co-section
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}q}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}I}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}+}}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}J}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}
.

Proof.

On objects, let
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}q}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}(({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}k}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}}))=({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}k}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}})
for
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}\leq{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}k}<{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}
.
A morphism
({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}k}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}})\to({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}l}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}})
is a length
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}l}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}
sequence with
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}k}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathbb{1}}
s, and we augment it by another
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathbb{1}}
on the
right
to get a length
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}l}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}2}
sequence with
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}k}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}2}

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathbb{1}}
s, hence a morphism
({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}k}+1{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}})\to({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}l}+1{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}})
.
A morphism
({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}k}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}})\to({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}l}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}})
is also a length
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}l}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}
sequence with
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}k}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathbb{1}}
s, but this time we augment it by a
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathbb{0}}
on the right to get a length
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}l}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}2}
sequence with
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}k}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathbb{1}}
s, hence a morphism
({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}k}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}})\to({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}l}+1{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}})
.
Finally, we send the new morphism
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\zeta}_{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}l}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}})}
to the sequence of
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}l}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathbb{0}}
s followed by one
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathbb{1}}
.
Functoriality is easy to check.
And to see that it is a discrete fibration, we observe that any binary sequence of length
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}l}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}2}
with a positive number of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathbb{1}}
s must be of exactly one of these three forms: a positive number of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathbb{1}}
s followed by a
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathbb{1}}
, a positive number of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathbb{1}}
s followed by a
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathbb{0}}
, or a sequence of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathbb{0}}
s followed by a
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\mathbb{1}}
.
∎

Evidently
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}q}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}}
restricts to
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}q}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}
as we shrink the categories.
Thus, we also get a relative isomorphism
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\partial\!{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\text{\char 136\relax}}}_{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}})}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}+}}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\partial\!{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\text{\char 136\relax}}}_{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}})}
over
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}q}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}
.

Now note that if we abstract over
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}b}
, the type of
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}t}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}
matches that of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}q}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}}
.
Thus, we can now prove by simultaneous induction that:

1.

{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}}\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Delta_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$-$}1}{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$-$}1}{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$\scriptstyle-$}1}{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}1}}}}}}
.

2.

{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Theta}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\partial\!{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\text{\char 136\relax}}}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}}}}\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\ell}
.

3.

{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}h}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}B}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}}}
.

4.

{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}t}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}q}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}}
.

We have already remarked that
1
and
3
are easy, and the base cases of
2
and
4
are likewise trivial.
For the induction step of
2
, we have

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}}~[~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x},~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}~]

\displaystyle\equiv({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}b}:\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}El}}~({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}h}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}-{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}))\to({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}X}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}){{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}\;{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}\;{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{,}}\;{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}t}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}b}\;{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}

\displaystyle\equiv({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}b}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}B}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}0}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x})\to{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Theta}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\partial\!{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\text{\char 136\relax}}}_{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}})}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}\;{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}\;{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{,}}\;{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}t}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}b}\;{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\ell}

\displaystyle\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Theta}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\partial\!{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\text{\char 136\relax}}}_{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}})}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}+}}}~[~{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\gamma}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}q}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}}~]\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\ell}

\displaystyle\equiv{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Theta}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\partial\!{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\text{\char 136\relax}}}_{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\boldsymbol{\rangle}})}}~[~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\partial}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x},~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x}~]\to\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}Type}}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\ell}.

Finally, the induction step of
4
follows immediately from the definition of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\gamma}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}p}
and the inductive hypothesis of
2
.
This completes the proof of the correctness of our construction of semi-simplicial types.

\triangleleft

5

Conclusion and Future Work

In this paper we have made two main contributions.
First, we have described
Displayed Type Theory (dTT)
, a new kind of type theory that incorporates (unary) internal parametricity but guarded by a modality, and showed that any model of dependent type theory with countable Reedy limits can be lifted to a model of dTT using augmented semi-simplicial diagrams.
Because the latter are diagrams on an
inverse
category, their type theory is more closely related to that of the original model, and indeed the original model sits inside our model of dTT at the discrete mode.
In particular, unlike other internally parametric type theories, dTT is compatible with classical axioms such as excluded middle and choice, as long as they are formulated at the discrete mode (or under the modality
{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\lozenge}}
), and can be used as an internal logic to reason about arbitrary
(\infty,1)
-toposes.

Secondly, inside dTT we have introduced a notion of
displayed coinductive type
, where the output of a destructor can be a parametricity ‘computability witness’ of the input, and showed that as a particular case of this notion we can define a type of
semi-simplicial types
.
This yields a new approach to the long-standing open problem of representing infinitely coherent higher structures in type theory.
Relative to other approaches, ours has the advantage that semi-simplicial types are defined (not postulated) as a simple instance of a type-former with natural introduction and elimination rules, i.e. a categorical universal property.
While it remains to be seen how much can actually be done in practice with our definition, early indications of its utility are promising.

There are a number of directions for future work suggested by our results; here we survey a few of them briefly.

5.0.0.1
Computation and implementation.

We conjecture that dTT satisfies canonicity and normalization, and should therefore be possible to implement in a proof assistant.

5.0.0.2
Modal internal parametricity.

We expect that most applications of ordinary internal parametricity have modal versions that can be proven in dTT (or a higher-ary version of it, as discussed below).
In addition to the traditional ‘free theorems’ such as those mentioned in the introduction, it would be especially interesting to investigate this for the proof of the pentagon identity for the smash product in
[
Cav21
]
, since such a proof would then apply internally to any
(\infty,1)
-topos.

5.0.0.3
Computing diamond.

Our intended semantic model strictly validates computation rules for diamond, such as
{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\lozenge}}~\left({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}\right)\equiv{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\lozenge}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}\to{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\lozenge}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}B}
, because type formers in the simplicial model extend type formers in the discrete model at the level of
({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}{\mathchoice{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$-$}1}{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$-$}1}{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$\scriptstyle-$}1}{\scalebox{0.6}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}1}}})
-simplices. The syntax of dTT may thus be augmented with computation rules for diamond. Formally, this would be accomplished in a manner similar to display, by extending the definition of diamond to meta-abstractions, such as to handle open terms under binders. One would introduce an operation,
troncature
(meaning
‘truncation’
in French), to model the action of diamond on telescopes. One then has:

\frac{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\Gamma},~\text{\faIconFromMacro{faLock}}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\lozenge}}\vdash_{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}sm}}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\Upsilon}\;\mathsf{tel}_{\;\!{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\ell}}}{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\Gamma}\vdash_{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}dm}}}{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\hbox{\hskip 3.75pt\hskip-3.75pt\hbox{\hbox{{$\lozenge$}}}\hskip-3.75pt\hskip-10.1389pt\raisebox{0.0pt}{\hbox{\rule{0.0pt}{0.0pt}\rule{0.0pt}{0.0pt}\hbox{\scalebox{0.5}{$\blacklozenge$}}}}\hskip-10.1389pt\hskip 3.75pt}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\Upsilon}\;\mathsf{tel}_{\;\!{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\ell}}}\frac{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\Gamma},~\text{\faIconFromMacro{faLock}}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\lozenge}}\vdash_{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}sm}}}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{A}}\left.\;\mathsf{type}_{\;\!{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\ell}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}1}}\middle/_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\upsilon}\;:\;{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\Upsilon}}\right.}{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\Gamma}\vdash_{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}dm}}}{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\lozenge}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathcal{A}}\left.\;\mathsf{type}_{\;\!{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\ell}_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}1}}\middle/_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\upsilon}^{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\flat}\;:\;{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\hbox{\hskip 2.625pt\hskip-2.625pt\hbox{\hbox{{$\lozenge$}}}\hskip-2.625pt\hskip-7.74307pt\raisebox{0.0pt}{\hbox{\rule{0.0pt}{0.0pt}\rule{0.0pt}{0.0pt}\hbox{\scalebox{0.5}{$\blacklozenge$}}}}\hskip-7.74307pt\hskip 2.625pt}}}\;{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\Upsilon}}\right.}

5.0.0.4
Higher category theory.

We have
defined
a type of semi-simplicial types in dTT, but such a definition is not an end in itself; it is intended as a tool for developing a theory of higher categories and other higher structures.
We hope that our corecursion principle of
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}
, and the availability of other displayed coinductive types for predicates and structures on them, should make the development of such a theory feasible in dTT.
We sketched some initial ideas in
sections

3.2
and
3.4
, but much remains to be done.

5.0.0.5
Elementary models.

In
section

4
we showed that any model of type theory with
\omega
-limits can be enhanced to a model of dTT including
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}
, but this is probably not the only way to construct models of dTT.
In particular, we conjecture that there are ‘realizability’ models of dTT in which
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}
is a classifier for ‘uniform’ semi-simplicial types.
This suggests that perhaps displayed coinductive types might be useful to include in a definition of elementary
(\infty,1)
-topos.

5.0.0.6
Higher-ary dTT.

The parametricity of dTT is
unary
, meaning that
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}
depends on one copy of
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}
; but parametricity in general can be
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}
-ary for any natural number
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}
, and some applications require higher arities.
We expect that higher-ary versions of dTT can be defined and modeled by a straightforward modification of the constructions in this paper, using higher-ary semi-cubical types in place of augmented semi-simplicial types (recall that augmented semi-simplicial types are the same as unary semi-cubical types).
In this case the binary numbers described in
section

4.2.1
become base-
({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}1})
numbers.

5.0.0.7
Symmetries.

In theories with non-modal internal parametricity, and also in Higher Observational Type Theory, it appears to be necessary to include a
‘symmetry’
operation on higher-dimensional types.
For instance, in our notation a symmetry operation would have the type
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}a_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 00$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}a_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}a_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}A}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}a_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 00$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}a_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 10$}}}~{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}a_{\scalebox{0.55}[1.0]{$\scriptscriptstyle 01$}}}
.
The absence of symmetry in dTT is a significant simplification; for instance, it means that
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\Delta^{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}+}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}op}}}}
is a strict inverse category, making possible the explicit syntactic model construction in
section

4.2
.
However, we have also seen that it leads to certain limitations, e.g. without symmetry it is unclear how to give a corecursion principle for
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}{{}^{\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}d}}}}
.

It should be possible to formulate a version of dTT (unary or higher-ary) with symmetry, but in the presence of symmetry it is unclear whether it is possible for display to compute definitionally on type-formers.
However, it should work to use either the interval-based style of
[
BM12
,
BCM15
,
Mou16
]
or the ‘observational’ style of
[
ACKS24
]
.

5.0.0.8
Unimode dTT.

We have formulated dTT with two modes, but intuitively the discrete mode is unnecessary, as the
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}dm}}
-types are embedded in the
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}sm}}
-types by the modality
{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}\triangle}}
.
Thus, it should be possible to formulate a version of dTT in which there is only one mode.
This is similar to other situations such as spatial/cohesive type theory
[
Shu18
]
and synthetic guarded domain theory
[
GKNB21
]
that have both unimodal and bimodal versions.

5.0.0.9
Conjectural syntax.

In addition to displayed coinductive types, one may consider other kinds of generalized inductive and coinductive types.
These are especially useful when taking a more ‘synthetic’ approach to higher structures in dTT, using the
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}sm}}
-types as augmented semi-simplicial objects rather than working with the internally defined type
\mathsf{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0}SST}}
of semi-simplicial types.

Firstly, regarding display as analogous to paths in homotopy type theory suggests
displayed inductive types
as analogues of higher inductive types.
Here the constructors generate displayed elements rather than ordinary ones.
